entities.summary:
Isidore of Kyiv, metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus' from 1437 to 1441, played a pivotal role in the medieval history of Eastern Europe. Born in unknown circumstances, he was chosen by Joseph II of Constantinople and served as the prelate of Byzantine Greek origin. During his tenure, he oversaw the unification of the Russian state and promoted the spread of Christianity. His legacy continued through the reign of Ivan III of Russia, who sought to emulate Isidore's diplomatic achievements. The city of Kiev, where Isidore resided, was a crucial center of trade and commerce, with the Don and Dnieper rivers serving as key transportation routes. The impact of Isidore's rule can be seen in the subsequent development of the Russian Orthodox Church and the establishment of Moscow as the primary city of Russia. As a prominent figure in the medieval period, Isidore of Kyiv left an indelible mark on the history of Eastern Europe, shaping the course of the Russian state and the spread of Christianity.

The causes of Isidore's significance include his appointment by Joseph II of Constantinople, which marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe. His role in unifying the Russian state also had far-reaching consequences, as it paved the way for the emergence of a unified Russian identity. Furthermore, Isidore's promotion of Christianity helped to spread the faith throughout Eastern Europe, leaving a lasting legacy in the region.

The effects of Isidore's rule were multifaceted, with his unification of the Russian state leading to increased trade and commerce, as well as the spread of Christianity. His diplomatic achievements also helped to establish Moscow as a major power in Eastern Europe, setting the stage for the rise of the Russian Empire. Additionally, Isidore's legacy continued through the reign of Ivan III of Russia, who sought to emulate his diplomatic achievements.
